questions.q: Which three components define a web origin?
questions.explain: Origin = scheme + domain + port. The path is not part of the origin.

questions.q: A page is loaded from http://normal-website.com/example/example.html. Which of these URLs are the SAME origin as that page?
questions.explain: Path doesn't matter, so the first two match. https changes both the scheme and the default port (443 vs 80). www is a different domain, because a subdomain is a separate origin. :8080 is a different port.

questions.q: Under the same-origin policy, a page can generally send requests to another origin, but its scripts can't read the responses.
questions.explain: Rule of thumb: send, yes; read, no. The browser attaches the user's cookies for the target domain, which is why reading must be blocked.

questions.q: The same-origin policy prevents a page from loading an image, video or script from another origin.
questions.explain: Cross-origin loading of resources (img, video, script tags) is generally allowed. SOP controls what the page's JavaScript can read from that content.

questions.q: Which cross-origin window property can a script WRITE but not READ?
questions.explain: location.href of a cross-origin iframe or new window is writable but not readable. window.length (number of frames) and closed are the reverse: readable but not writable.

questions.q: Pages on marketing.example.com and example.com want to relax the SOP between them using document.domain. What is required?
choices: Only the marketing.example.com page sets document.domain = 'example.com'
Only the example.com page sets document.domain = 'marketing.example.com'
questions.explain: Both sides must set it to the same value, and that value must be part of their FQDN. Setting it to a TLD like 'com' used to work, but modern browsers block it.

questions.q: Cookies set by a site are often accessible from all of its subdomains, even though each subdomain is a separate origin.
questions.explain: For legacy reasons, SOP is looser for cookies. The HttpOnly flag partly mitigates this.

questions.q: Which request header does the browser add to a cross-origin request to tell the server where the request came from?
questions.explain: The browser sends Origin, and the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

questions.q: When does the browser let a page read the response to a cross-origin request?
choices: When the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header matches the requesting origin
When the request was sent with the Origin header
When the response sets a cookie for the requesting origin
questions.explain: The browser compares ACAO with the requesting origin and lets the page read the response only if they match.

questions.q: Which of these Access-Control-Allow-Origin values will browsers actually accept as valid?
questions.explain: A single origin, null, or * are valid. A wildcard can't be part of another value, so https://*.normal-website.com is invalid. The spec lists multiple origins, but no browser supports them.

questions.q: A server may respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
questions.explain: That combination is not permitted because it would expose authenticated content to every site.

questions.q: A script sets xhr.withCredentials = true. The server replies with a matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin but no Access-Control-Allow-Credentials header. What happens?
choices: The browser doesn't let the page read the response
The page can read the response, but cookies are stripped from it
The browser retries the request without credentials
The page can read the response normally
questions.explain: For a credentialed request, the server must return Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, or the browser won't expose the response to the page.

questions.q: Why do some servers build Access-Control-Allow-Origin dynamically by copying the client's Origin header?
choices: Because * can't be combined with credentials, so they echo the origin to allow authenticated access
Because browsers ignore ACAO unless it matches the Host header
Because the spec requires ACAO to be generated per request
questions.explain: Echoing the origin gets around the wildcard-plus-credentials restriction, but it is insecure: it trusts every origin.

questions.q: Name the CORS response header that must be set to true before a page can read the response to a request sent with cookies.
questions.explain: By default, cross-origin requests go without credentials (cookies, Authorization header, client certificates). The server opts in with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

questions.q: Which HTTP method does the browser use for a CORS pre-flight request?
questions.explain: The pre-flight is an OPTIONS request that asks whether the real request's method and headers are allowed.

questions.q: Why were pre-flight checks added to CORS?
choices: To protect legacy resources from the extra request options that CORS allows
To stop CSRF attacks from HTML forms
To let servers set cookies on other origins
questions.explain: Older servers weren't built to expect cross-origin requests with non-standard methods or headers. The pre-flight asks permission first.

questions.q: Which headers does the BROWSER send in a pre-flight request?
questions.explain: The browser sends Origin plus the Request-Method and Request-Headers it wants to use. Allow-Methods and Max-Age are headers the server sends back in its response.

questions.q: What does the Access-Control-Max-Age response header control?
choices: How long the pre-flight response may be cached and reused
How long the session cookie stays valid
How many cross-origin requests a client may make
How long the browser waits for the real response
questions.explain: Caching the pre-flight response saves the extra round-trip on later requests.

questions.q: A pre-flight check can be triggered when a cross-origin request uses a non-standard HTTP method or non-standard headers.
questions.explain: For example, a PUT with a custom header triggers an OPTIONS pre-flight before the real request.

questions.q: Pre-flight checks add no overhead, because the browser sends them in the same round-trip as the real request.
questions.explain: The pre-flight is a separate OPTIONS round-trip that happens before the real request, so it adds overhead.

questions.q: To avoid maintaining a whitelist, a server copies any Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and also sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. What is the consequence?
choices: Any website can read responses generated in the victim's session, such as API keys and CSRF tokens
Only subdomains of the server can read responses
Responses can be read, but without the victim's cookies
Nothing, because the browser still enforces the same-origin policy
questions.explain: Reflecting the origin with credentials trusts every domain. An attacker's page can make a credentialed XHR and exfiltrate responseText.

questions.q: A server trusts any origin that ENDS WITH normal-website.com. Which attacker origin passes this check?
questions.explain: hackersnormal-website.com ends with the trusted string, and an attacker can register it. The .evil-user.net domain would beat a 'begins with' check instead.

questions.q: A server trusts any origin that BEGINS WITH https://normal-website.com. Which attacker origin passes this check?
questions.explain: The attacker controls evil-user.net and can create a normal-website.com subdomain under it. Prefix, suffix and regex matching of origins is easy to get wrong.

questions.q: In which situations do browsers send Origin: null?
choices: Ordinary requests from a subdomain of the target
questions.explain: A subdomain sends its own origin (e.g. https://www.normal-website.com), not null.

questions.q: Why do developers often add the null origin to a CORS whitelist?
choices: To allow requests from mobile apps over HTTPS
questions.explain: Local files (file:) send Origin: null, so null gets whitelisted for convenience. Attackers can produce that same null origin.

questions.q: A server responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. How can an attacker's page make the victim's browser send Origin: null?
choices: Run the exploit script inside a sandboxed iframe whose content is a data: URL
Set the Origin header to null manually with setRequestHeader
Send the request over plain HTTP instead of HTTPS
Use an img tag instead of XHR
questions.explain: A sandboxed iframe (sandbox='allow-scripts allow-top-navigation allow-forms') gets an opaque origin, so its credentialed XHR carries Origin: null. Scripts can't set the Origin header themselves.

questions.q: In a CORS exploit script, which XMLHttpRequest property does the attacker set to true so that the victim's cookies are sent with the request?
questions.explain: Cross-origin requests are sent without cookies unless the script opts in with withCredentials = true.

questions.q: An API correctly trusts only https://subdomain.vulnerable-website.com, but that subdomain has an XSS vulnerability. What can an attacker do?
choices: Inject JavaScript on the subdomain that makes CORS requests to the API and steals sensitive data such as an API key
Nothing, because a correct whitelist makes XSS on trusted origins irrelevant
Only deface the subdomain, with no effect on the API
Read the API's data only if the API also has XSS
questions.explain: CORS creates trust between origins. XSS on a trusted origin lets the attacker run code as that origin and use its CORS access.

questions.q: A CORS configuration that lists only exact, legitimate origins can still be exploited if one of those origins is vulnerable.
questions.explain: If a trusted origin is compromised (for example through XSS), the attacker inherits its trust.

questions.q: An HTTPS-only app whitelists http://trusted-subdomain.vulnerable-website.com (plain HTTP). What must an attacker be able to do to exploit this?
choices: Find XSS on the main HTTPS site
Steal the server's TLS private key
questions.explain: The attacker injects a redirect to the trusted HTTP origin, intercepts that plain-HTTP request, and serves a spoofed page that makes the CORS request to the HTTPS app.

questions.q: In the TLS-breaking attack, which Origin header does the victim's browser send with the CORS request to https://vulnerable-website.com?
questions.explain: The spoofed page is served as if it came from the whitelisted HTTP origin, so the browser reports that origin and the app allows it.

questions.q: Whitelisting a plain-HTTP subdomain is harmless as long as the main site has no HTTP endpoints and all of its cookies are marked Secure.
questions.explain: The attack works even when the site is otherwise solid on HTTPS. The weak point is the trusted HTTP origin, which a MITM attacker can impersonate.

questions.q: Why do most CORS attacks require Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true?
choices: Without it, the browser doesn't send the victim's cookies, so the attacker only gets content they could fetch directly anyway
Without it, the browser blocks all cross-origin requests
Without it, the server can't read the Origin header
Without it, pre-flight requests always fail
questions.explain: Uncredentialed responses contain no session-specific data, unless the attacker couldn't reach the resource in the first place (intranets).

questions.q: intranet.normal-website.com responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and no credentials. Why is this still dangerous?
choices: An external site visited by an internal user can use that user's browser as a proxy to read intranet resources the attacker can't reach directly
The wildcard makes the browser send intranet cookies to every site
The wildcard disables TLS on the intranet
It isn't dangerous, because no credentials are involved
questions.explain: Private IP space is unreachable from outside, and internal sites are often held to lower security standards. A victim's browser inside the network bridges that gap.

questions.q: Which of these are recommended ways to prevent CORS vulnerabilities?
choices: List trusted origins explicitly in Access-Control-Allow-Origin for resources with sensitive data
Reflect the Origin header so every legitimate client works
Rely on CORS instead of server-side authentication
questions.explain: Reflecting Origin without validation trusts everyone. CORS only defines browser behavior, so it doesn't replace authentication or session management.

questions.q: A strict CORS policy can replace server-side authentication and access control for sensitive data.
questions.explain: CORS only controls what browsers let pages read. An attacker can forge a request with any Origin directly from their own client, so the server must still authenticate requests and manage sessions.

questions.q: Why isn't network configuration alone enough to protect internal resources that send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *?
choices: Browsers on the internal network can also visit untrusted external sites, which can then reach internal resources through them
Wildcards are ignored by internal browsers
Internal resources are always reachable from the public internet
questions.explain: The victim's browser sits inside the network perimeter and can run scripts from outside it.

questions.q: A correctly configured CORS policy protects a site against CSRF.
questions.explain: This is a common misconception. CORS relaxes the SOP rather than adding protection. CSRF works without CORS, for example through simple HTML forms or cross-domain resource includes.

questions.q: How can a poorly configured CORS policy affect CSRF risk?
choices: It can increase the possibility or impact of CSRF
It has no relationship to CSRF
It only affects CSRF over plain HTTP
questions.explain: Because CORS relaxes the SOP, overly lenient settings can let attacker pages read responses (such as CSRF tokens), which makes CSRF attacks easier or more damaging.
